newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton-Futures now a reality, says trade.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-Futures now a reality, says trade.

text.p: Cotton futures trading in India, suspended 30 years ago, will now be a reality with the federal cabinet approving the proposal, traders said on Thursday.
"We welcome the government's decision. It will help farmers, traders and mills," said a trader.

Traders said the East India Cotton Association (EICA) and South India Cotton Association (SICA), both trade representative organisations had shown interest in setting up facilities for futures trading.
Forward trading in cotton was banned in the 1960s in a bid to curb speculation and to stabilise prices.
Traders said they would expect futures trading to take off by December or early next year as it invloved the setting up of infrastructure facilities.
"It will take some time to set up the facilities required to carry out forward trading in cotton as they involve a modern computer network," said Manubhai Amarsey, a leading trader.
"It also needs a lot of investment," he said.
Traders said the government's decision to allow cotton futures trading initially for three years would not help the very purpose of introducing such a facility.
"The government must amend its decision and allow futures trading on a permanent basis. Otherwise, who will invest in a temporary facility?" a trader asked.
"Farmers can realise higher prices through selling forward, traders can cover their price risks, mills can buy in advance and exporters can book their stocks in advance," a trader said.
In the week to Thursday, cotton prices were mixed as the varieties from India's western state of Gujarat recovered while those from the northern state of Punjab suffered losses.
The Gujarat varieties firmed on reports that there had been crop losses due to recent floods, they said.
There was also some speculative buying in the wake of the Indian cabinet's approval for a proposal to allow futures trading in cotton.
"Cotton buying from yarn mills remained poor but speculative activity helped prices firm," one trader said.
"The government has allowed forward trading in cotton after a lapse of 30 years and traders are gearing up to commence forward trading," he said.
In spot, Gujarat Kalyan rose 200 rupees to 14,000/14,200 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and wagad cotton 300 rupees to 13,000 rupees per candy.
Long-staple Gujarat Sankar-4 gained 400/500 rupees to 17,000/18,000 rupees per candy for the average variety and 19,500/20,500 rupees for the superior variety.
The Punjab varieties remained subdued due to selling by traders triggered by a satisfactory progress of monsoon rains.
Punjab saw-ginned fell 10/25 rupees to 1,800/1,850 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). Bengal-deshi fell 10/30 rupees to 995/1,045 rupees per maund.
Traders said the overall progress of the four-month June-September monsoon had been satisfactory.
"Looking at the progress of the monsoon, sluggish mill buying, absence of a fresh export quota and unsold stock, I expect cotton prices to remain subdued in the coming days," Amarsey said.
